analysis.one_liner: Eliminates capital gains and estate taxes, cuts the corporate rate to 12.5%, and cancels unspent stimulus and TARP authority.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Jim Jordan with 49 Republican cosponsors, was referred to three House committees in April 2010 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have eliminated all federal taxes on capital gains for individuals and corporations, cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 12.5%, let businesses deduct the full cost of equipment immediately, and made the estate tax repeal permanent. It would have also halved payroll tax rates for 2010, canceled unspent funds from the 2009 stimulus law, repealed parts of that law including COBRA health-insurance help for the unemployed and aid to state governments, ended the government's authority to make new Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) investments, and required the Treasury to sell its TARP bank stock.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors, corporations, and heirs of large estates would gain the most: no capital gains tax, a corporate rate of 12.5%, unlimited expensing of equipment, and permanent estate tax repeal. Workers would get a one-year cut in their payroll tax (Social Security's 6.2% employee rate dropping to 3.1% for 2010), and businesses would pay less in payroll tax for 2010. Bank shareholders would benefit from the government being required to sell its TARP stakes.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals and corporations would pay a 0% rate on capital gains, including under the alternative minimum tax, effective for tax years after 2009.
The maximum corporate income tax rate would drop to 12.5%, from 35%.
Businesses could deduct the entire cost of depreciable assets and software in the year purchased, permanently and without a dollar cap.
The estate and generation-skipping transfer tax repeal would be made permanent instead of expiring at the end of 2010.
Employee, employer, and self-employment payroll tax rates would be roughly halved for calendar year 2010.
Unobligated stimulus funds would be canceled, TARP's authority to make new investments would terminate, and Treasury would have to sell all TARP stock and warrants within a year.
The bill would repeal the 2009 stimulus law's limits on executive compensation for rescued firms and its health information technology, state fiscal relief, broadband, TANF, and COBRA provisions.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall sharply from the permanent elimination of capital gains, corporate (in part), and estate taxes, plus the one-year payroll tax cut. Social Security and Medicare would see reduced payroll tax funding for 2010. Unemployed workers relying on COBRA premium assistance, state governments relying on fiscal relief, TANF-funded programs, broadband expansion projects, and health-IT programs funded through Medicare and Medicaid would lose their remaining stimulus support.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal revenue, Social Security/Medicare funding, stimulus programs

drawbacks.text: Halving payroll tax rates for 2010 would cut the dedicated funding stream for Social Security and Medicare by roughly half for that year.

The bill would cancel unspent stimulus money and repeal COBRA premium assistance for laid-off workers, state fiscal relief, TANF emergency funds, and Medicare/Medicaid health-IT incentives, ending programs mid-stream.

Permanently eliminating capital gains and estate taxes and cutting the corporate rate would reduce federal revenue substantially with no offset, adding to deficits; the benefits would flow disproportionately to households that own capital assets and large estates.
Ending TARP authority outright would remove the government's emergency lending and investment tools while the financial system was still recovering from the 2008 crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers very large, permanent tax cuts aimed at capital income and corporate profits, plus a genuine one-year tax cut for workers, and pays for none of it. Its savings come from canceling remaining stimulus aid, including COBRA health-insurance help for the unemployed and support for state budgets, and from dismantling TARP. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge the arithmetic: permanent trillions-scale tax cuts offset by temporary, targeted spending cancellations. As a pure growth prescription it rests on the argument that lower taxes on investment spur job creation; as a fiscal document it is a large redistribution toward capital.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2010 and split between the Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Appropriations committees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died there when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, joined by Rep. Jason Chaffetz, introduced the Economic Freedom Act of 2010 on April 15, 2010.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Appropriations committees the day it was introduced.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup appears in the record, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, investors, corporations, and large estates did not receive the tax cuts, while the remaining stimulus programs, COBRA assistance for unemployed workers, state aid, and TARP authority were left in place. Workers also did not get the promised one-year payroll tax cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Stimulus programs kept running; investors got no tax cut

for.name: Jim Jordan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled Republican cosponsors.

for.name: Jason Chaffetz
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Appropriations Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or committee vote appears in the record, so the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 50 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill in the record, and the Democratic-controlled House never acted on it.

industries.industry: Investors and holders of capital gains and large estates
industries.note: The bill would eliminate capital gains and estate taxes permanently, a benefit concentrated in households with significant assets. The cost is forgone federal revenue that would otherwise fund public programs.
A 12.5% corporate rate and unlimited immediate expensing would sharply cut business tax bills. Workers would share in the 2010 payroll tax cut, but the permanent gains flow to capital.

industries.industry: Banks and firms that received TARP investments
industries.note: The bill would terminate TARP's authority and force Treasury to sell the government's bank stock and warrants within a year, ending government ownership stakes. It would also repeal executive-pay limits imposed on rescued firms.
Repealing the stimulus law's Medicare and Medicaid health-IT programs would end subsidy-funded demand for electronic records systems. Their loss would be federal savings.
Repealing state fiscal relief would leave states covering budget shortfalls on their own, typically through service cuts or tax increases that land on residents.
Repealing the stimulus law's broadband technology programs would cancel remaining federal funding for expansion projects.
